Why the sky appears blue due to Rayleigh scattering of sunlight

Would you recognize the sky on another planet?

We're so used to Earth's blue sky that it can feel almost universal. It isn't.

On Mercury, there is essentially no atmosphere to scatter sunlight the way Earth's atmosphere does. So despite the intense sunlight, the sky would appear black even during the day.

On Venus, a massive carbon-dioxide atmosphere and thick sulfuric-acid clouds completely transform the view. Near the surface, sunlight is heavily filtered and scattered, creating a dim, yellowish-orange, hazy environment — nothing like Earth's open blue sky.

On Earth, molecules in the atmosphere scatter shorter blue wavelengths more strongly, giving us our familiar blue sky. At sunset, sunlight travels through a much longer path through the atmosphere, making reds and oranges more prominent.
